The cat could have done it, in the way cats do things. The baker's warmth could have swelled the wood.

She pumps the pedals once, gently, and the sigh that comes out is no longer quite a sigh. It has an edge, the beginning of a vowel. She stops pumping at once, and the sound hangs in the room a moment after the bellows go slack.

She does not push the knob back in. She sits with her shoes off on the warm board and does not decide whether the gap is an answer, an asking, or only wood.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The baker's oven flues run up through the loft wall, and the brick is old and thin. On a still morning anyone standing at the flue grate downstairs can hear the schoolroom clearly, like a speaking tube nobody installed. The baker has known this for twenty years and says nothing about it. The school has always been quiet at the start of the day, which he took for good manners. It was partly that he was listening.

**Consequence of yours:** Hester sits shoeless on the warm board with the half-drawn stop and the unfinished vowel still hanging in the room, and the board carries more than heat. She feels the ovens' tick and shift through her heels, and under it the slow roll of dough being worked, so that she is aware, without turning her head, that the baker is at his table just below her.

He has heard it too. At the grate, hands floured to the wrists, he stops kneading at the first edge of the vowel. It is not a word, but it is a mouth getting ready for one. He remains there longer than the dough can afford. A man who once signed a book he shouldn't have, and then broke a silence with a true sentence, is not alarmed by the sound of something almost speaking.

Above, Hester takes her hand off the pedal. Below, he doesn't move. Neither knows the other is listening, and the ovens go on ticking in the quiet between.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The flue grate in the baker's wall is also an asking place, though nobody has ever put anything on it. It has a ledge exactly the width of a hand, worn smooth by flour. A stranger would read it as a shelf. Marrowby children, who know every sill, avoid it without being told, because a thing left there would be seen by no one and answered by no one.

**Consequence of yours:** The baker's stillness at the grate lasts only until the dough starts to sag. Then, for the first time in twenty years, he puts something on the ledge: a small roll, still warm, just out of the oven. He doesn't think about it. His hands do it while his mind is above his head, listening to a board that has stopped moving.

The roll sits on the flour-worn ledge, and the heat from it rises a few inches and meets the grate's draft, which carries the smell of bread up the flue and into the loft. Hester, shoeless on the warm board, smells bread that has not been delivered. She does not connect it with the vowel. She thinks only that it's a good morning for baking and that she has not eaten.

Under the grate the roll cools. Nobody touches it. By the rules that apply to sills, it has asked a question, and the room above it, which could answer by pulling the stop, only breathes in.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** By the old sill custom, any creature may answer. A touch from a child, a stray dog, or a gull counts as much as one from the person the question was meant for, and the asker is not entitled to know which. The rule was made so that no one could be refused by silence alone, and it has worked well enough that most people have forgotten it was ever a rule. Gulls, for their part, have not been informed.

**Consequence of yours:** The roll cools on the ledge for about the length of the schoolroom's morning. Then Biscuit, who lives in the bakery by the town's reckoning and glares at the loft by his own, comes through the back door on his unhurried rounds and sees it at nose height. He considers it the way he considers everything, as a matter between himself and the universe. He eats half. He leaves the rest, and a few crumbs, and goes upstairs to sit on the harmonium's lid.

The baker, coming back to the grate with floured hands, finds a half-eaten roll and a ledge that has been answered. He has no way of knowing whether the answer came from the cat, from Hester, or from something older that the ledge was made for. He looks at it for some time. He does not clear it away, and he does not eat the rest. Above him the vowel does not come again, and the cat, having done what cats do, begins to wash.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** Marrowby's gulls are not fed by anyone, but they have a schedule. Each morning, one gull lands on the harbor wall at the sparrows' stone, drinks from the seaward edge, and leaves before the first fisherman arrives. It is always the same bird, recognizable by a notch in one wing. The sparrows allow this. The town calls it "the Inspector" and treats it as faintly official.

**Consequence of yours:** The half-eaten roll stays on the ledge into the afternoon, and the baker, who has stopped trying to decide what it means, goes about his work around it. The first customer to see it is a boy sent for a loaf, who stops at the grate, looks at the roll, and looks at the baker. The baker, floured to the elbows, says "it's on the sill." The boy nods, accepting this as a complete explanation, and takes his loaf. Within the hour three people have used the phrase about the roll, and none of them knows where it came from.

Upstairs, Hester hears the phrase carried up the flue in pieces. She hears "sill," then "roll." She does not know it is about bread, and has just written the other half of a thought in her notebook. It says "the voice that was removed." She underlines nothing. The cat, finished washing, goes to sleep on the lid, a quarter-tone above the bell, and she does not move him.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The Inspector comes only on mornings that will stay dry. On days a flood is coming, the stone is left to the sparrows, and the gull is not seen at all. Nobody has proved this, but the fishermen swear by it, and a few have taken to checking the wall before deciding whether to carry coats. The Inspector has never been wrong that anyone could prove, and the town, which is wary of anything that claims to know in advance, has made an exception for a bird.

**Consequence of yours:** Because the town treats the Inspector as faintly official, the Clerk, who has an empty ledger and a great deal of free time, finds himself walking to the wall at dawn. The gull lands, drinks, and goes. The Clerk, uncertain why, takes out his ledger and writes: "Inspector, one visit, drank." It is the first entry in months, and it is not a flood. There is no column for it. He writes it in the margin.

Corvin, passing with his thermos, sees the line and doesn't object. The fund pays per flood under a named author, and this is neither a flood nor authored. The Clerk looks at the entry for a while, then writes "dry" beside it, which is a word he has not used in the ledger before. He doesn't know whether the book will accept it. The Inspector, already gone, has left a small, wet print on the seaward edge of the stone.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The wet print on the stone is a footprint, and it is the wrong shape for a gull. It has four toes, not three, and a short heel pad, closer to a small dog's or a fox's than a bird's. By the time the Clerk looks again the sun has dried it, and the stone is plain. Nobody else saw it, so it exists only in the margin where he writes: "print, not gull's, gone."

**Consequence of yours:** "Dry" in the Clerk's margin begins a second, unofficial ledger. Corvin does not mention it, but he starts reading the margins when he passes the bench, the way the town reads the sky. Within a week there are a dozen entries in the Clerk's crabbed hand: "Inspector, drank, dry." "No Inspector, sparrows only, slush by noon." "Duck unchanged." None of them is a fee, and none is signed or witnessed, and the Clerk, who has spent his life under the two-witness rule, finds he likes writing things down that nobody has to believe.

The fishermen start glancing at the bench before they glance at the wall. Whether the margin is now more reliable than the bird, or just a bird's reputation passed through a second set of hands, nobody says. The print goes in once, as a question, and the Clerk does not write it again.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The eel-sellers keep the town's cat pairings in their heads and speak them only as prices. "A penny the pair" means a cat and its rival house are in balance. "Tuppence" means the rivalry is live. "Free" means a cat has no pairing at all, and the eel-sellers say it with an odd carefulness, since in Marrowby a cat with no rival is considered a little unlucky for the street it sleeps on.

**Consequence of yours:** The Clerk, with the four-toed print in his margin, recognizes the shape from the other side of his own life. A cat's print has four toes and no claw marks, a dog's has claws, and a fox's is longer. It was a cat, and no cat in Marrowby drinks at the sparrows' stone, since the stone is the sparrows' and every cat knows it. So he walks to the eel stalls at noon and asks, in the plainest words he can manage, which cat might have been on the wall at dawn.

The eel-seller, wiping a knife, says "free." The Clerk waits for more and none comes. A cat with no home and no rival is on the wall at dawn, drinking where the Inspector drinks, and the one trade that has never been suspected of anything has just told him so in a price. He buys an eel to be polite. He writes nothing in the margin, which for him is a decision, and the sparrows' stone is dry and plain when he passes it on the way home.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The free cat is not new. The eel-sellers have said "free" about the same unnamed cat for eleven years, to anyone who asked, and nobody did. It is a small, tortoiseshell cat with one ear folded forward, and it has never been seen eating anything the town put out. It sleeps in the customs house porch, the one threshold the other cats won't cross. Nobody has thought to connect the two facts, because the porch is a place people pass through and don't look at.

**Consequence of yours:** The Clerk's eel, bought to be polite, is eaten on the harbor wall, and it is a good one. As he eats he looks at the porch of the customs house across the water, small on its hill, and thinks about the one building every cat in town has left out of its pairings. He does not draw the conclusion. He draws only a line in the margin: a short mark, not a word. Corvin, who reads margins now, stops over it that evening and cannot decide whether it is a mistake or a placeholder.

Neither man mentions the cat. In the morning the Clerk goes up the hill with half an eel in a paper twist and sets it on the porch step. It is, by the sill custom, a question. He does not wait to see who answers, and the doorframe above him, warm at shoulder height, is not in any sun.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** Marrowby has an old belief that tortoiseshell cats know which lies are about to be told. Nobody has tested it, and the town doesn't quite hold it, but a few people won't tell a small lie in front of one. The belief is not repeated in front of children, since they might try to test it, and the one who did, years ago, said only that the cat had looked at her for a long time and gone to sleep.

**Consequence of yours:** The cat does not eat the eel. That is no surprise, since it has never been seen eating anything the town put out, and by the sill rule, untouched is a slow answer and not a rude one. But when the Clerk returns that evening, out of breath, the paper twist has moved. It is a hand's width to the left, off the step and onto the worn stone beside it, with the eel still inside, folded over once, as if someone had set it aside to make room.

He stands there longer than the walk up justified. The cat is asleep on the far side of the porch with its folded ear toward him. He reads the answer as best he can: touched, not taken. In the margin he writes, "touched," and for the first time has no wish to explain it. The twist stays where it is. By morning it is gone, and the stone is clean, and nobody has seen who.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The customs house has a second door, on the north side, that is bricked up. The brick is newer than the walls and has no mortar date. Nobody knows when it was sealed or why, and the single open door, the one that must stay unlocked, was the only one the charter ever mentioned. A thin line of moss runs along the bottom of the bricks, and in dry weather a small, regular gap appears under the lowest course, about the height of a cat.

**Consequence of yours:** The eel has gone, and the Clerk goes back up the hill on the third evening with nothing in his hands. He has no offering and no question. He circles the building for the first time in his life and finds the north wall, the bricks, the moss, and the gap. Something warm and low-lying has worn a faint track in the grass leading to it, narrow enough for one animal at a time.

He crouches, which his knees dislike, and does not put his hand near the gap. He sets nothing on the ground. In the margin that night he writes "north side, bricked, a gap," then crosses out "a gap" and writes "a way in." Corvin, who has counted the fund below that wall thirty times, reads the line and finds he knows exactly where the cellar draft has been coming from, and is not yet ready to say so.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The locked fund box has not been moved in anyone's memory. It stands against the cellar's north wall on four small stone pads, and the floor beneath it is paler than the rest, as if it had been swept more often. Nobody sweeps there. The yearly count is made by opening the lid, and the lid is hinged at the back, so it has never needed the box to be turned or lifted.

**Consequence of yours:** Corvin, who has been waiting to be ready, goes down to the cellar with a candle and his scarf and does not count anything. He holds the candle at arm's length and watches the flame lean, steadily, toward the north wall, toward the box. The draft is strongest there. The smell of low tide is strongest there. On the other side of that wall, he now knows, is the sealed door, the moss, and a gap the height of a cat.

He puts one hand flat on the box's lid, as he has for thirty years, and for the first time notices that it is cold, not warm like the frame upstairs. He does not try to move it. He thinks about the fund's clause, the repair of the harbor wall, and about two assents, and about what the surplus is guarding in a room where nothing said can flood. Then he takes up the candle and counts the money, which is, as always, exactly right, and writes down the total.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The fund's annual total has never changed. In thirty years of Corvin's counts, and in every count recorded in the ledger before him, the surplus has been the same figure to the penny, though the charter says interest is added each year and fees are paid out. The ledger carries no entries for interest, and none for withdrawals beyond the Clerk's fees, which are accounted for somewhere else. Nobody has ever reconciled the two books, because they are kept in different hands and read at different times.

**Consequence of yours:** Corvin writes down the total and, for the first time in thirty years, reads the line above it. It is identical, to the penny, and so is the line above that. He turns pages back, slowly, with the cellar draft lifting the corner of each, and the number does not move. A fund that never earns and never pays out should be a locked box, but a box that holds exactly the same sum for generations, in a room with a draft that smells of tide, is something else. He doesn't know what.

He closes the ledger and sets his palm on the cold lid again. He could ask the Clerk, who has the other book, but the Clerk is whittling, and a question put to a man who has just learned to say "dry" is a question that might get an answer. Corvin is not sure he wants one yet. He climbs the stair, touches the warm doorframe on the way out, and does not note that he did.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The Clerk has never thrown away a fee wrapper. His fees arrive as a small packet of exact coins in plain brown paper, left on his bench without a note, and he has kept every wrapper, folded flat, in the drawer where the better duck used to be. There are several hundred. The paper is oddly good, thick and faintly damp-smelling, and he saves it because it seemed wasteful to burn. He has never asked who leaves them, since the money was always correct.

**Consequence of yours:** Corvin does eventually ask the Clerk, a day later and on the wall, with the thermos between them as an excuse. "Who pays your fees?" he says. "You do," says the Clerk, "in the packets." Corvin says he has never made one up, and the Clerk says he has never said he did. Both are true, and the harbor stays flat.

Neither moves. The Inspector, who has come and gone, has left the sparrows' stone dry. The Clerk opens the drawer that evening and counts wrappers by lamplight, and at the bottom finds the oldest, creased soft as cloth, with a faint tide-line stain across one corner. He lays it beside the newest. They match exactly. He closes the drawer and the entry in his margin reads only "packets, same hand," and he does not write whose.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** Tobias Quill carries a parcel to the customs house porch on the first Thursday of every month, wrapped in the same thick brown paper and addressed only "the Hill." It was handed to him by the ferryman before him, along with the knot, and he has never opened it, asked who sends it, or checked whether anyone collects it. He leaves it on the step. On the next crossing it is always gone, and the step is clean.

**Consequence of yours:** The Clerk takes the oldest wrapper to the ferry slip and holds it out to Tobias without a question. Tobias looks at it with his good ear turned the other way, which is how he looks at everything, and says "that's the Hill's paper." He says it with no weight, as a man might say that is a Tuesday. The Clerk asks how he knows, and Tobias says it is the same as the parcels, and that he has never thought about it because it was never his to think about.

The Clerk folds the wrapper and puts it back in his pocket. First Thursday is four days off. He does not decide to be on the hill that evening, and he does not decide not to. The yellow boat sits at the slip, tied with the one that holds, and the water under it is quite still.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The parcel is never handed to Tobias. On the first Thursday of each month he finds it already on the ferry's bow, under the tallow lantern, tied in the one that holds, with the knot's third move looking wrong in exactly the usual way. He has always assumed the ferryman before him started the custom and that someone in town carries it on. He has never asked who, and in sixty years the question has not once occurred to him until this week.

**Consequence of yours:** The Clerk's wrapper has made the parcel heavier. On the first Thursday Tobias finds it at dawn and, for the first time, picks it up and weighs it in both hands, like a man guessing the age of a stranger. It is lighter than he remembers, or he is stronger, or his memory has been kind. He carries it up the hill himself instead of sending the boy, and at the bend before the customs house he stops, because the Clerk is already sitting on the low wall there with half an eel in a paper twist, looking as though he had arrived by accident.

Neither says why. Tobias sets the parcel on his knee. The Clerk sets the twist beside it. Across the path, in the porch's shadow, the tortoiseshell cat with the folded ear sits upright and watches them both, not hurrying, with the manner of someone expecting two letters and getting one.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The tortoiseshell cat is not alone in the porch. A second, much older animal lives in the same shadow, a very large, very still grey cat, so old that its fur has the texture of felt and its eyes are the same pale color as the fund-box lid. It has never moved while anyone watched. Eleven years ago a child called it "the stone," and the name stuck because it was indistinguishable from one. The tortoiseshell sleeps against its flank.

**Consequence of yours:** The two men and the parcel sit in the bend of the path with the cat looking on, and neither knows what to do with the other's presence. Tobias, who has the parcel and no reason to be on the hill, says "it's the first Thursday," which is true. The Clerk, who has the twist and no reason to be on the hill, says "it's the eel's day," which is not, and nothing floods, because nobody has ever been on a hill where the tide doesn't reach.

Then the stone moves. One ear turns, the width of a finger, toward the parcel. The tortoiseshell lifts its head. Tobias, feeling the weight on his knee change, does not look down. The Clerk, watching the porch, sees what Tobias cannot: the stone's eyes, pale as the lid, resting on the knot. The one that holds. The third move, the wrong one, and the old animal looking at it as if it had been waiting sixty years to see it tied correctly.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The eel-sellers have a price for every cat in Marrowby, including the free one. They have no price for the stone. Asked about the large grey animal in the porch, they say nothing at all, which in a trade that speaks only in prices is a very loud silence. A child once asked what it would cost, and an eel-seller wrapped her purchase and gave her change for a coin she hadn't handed over.

**Consequence of yours:** Tobias, who cannot see the porch from where he sits, feels the Clerk go still and says, with his good ear turned toward him, "Is it looking?" The Clerk says yes. "What at?" says Tobias. "The knot," says the Clerk. Tobias nods slowly and looks at the parcel on his knee as though it had spoken. "The ferryman before me said the third move was the only part that was right. I always thought he meant the opposite."

They finish the walk together. Tobias sets the parcel on the step in the old way, the Clerk sets the twist beside it, and the tortoiseshell stands and sniffs the knot without touching it. Then both men sit down on the low wall to see who takes it. Dusk comes, and the gold light of Alder's lantern starts its first round of the wall, far below. The parcel is still on the step when they leave, the first one in sixty years that has not been taken within the hour, and neither man says whether that is an answer or only slowness.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The parcel is heavy with something small. When Tobias leaves it on the step, the weight shifts in the paper, as if something inside has settled. It is not loose coin and it is not tools. It is slightly warm, in a way no one has noticed because it was always collected within the hour, and warmth in Marrowby is attributed to the sun.

**Consequence of yours:** The two men go down the hill in the dusk and, at the bend, run into Alder Finch starting his round. He stops, lantern raised, and looks at them with the mild suspicion of a man who has been up all night for forty years and does not expect company before midnight. He has the knot in his pocket, still, and the Clerk and Tobias, between them, have a parcel left on a step and an animal that did not take it.

Alder hums four flat notes without knowing it. Tobias, who has heard them nightly for sixty years and never once placed them, says "that's the knot," and hums them back, a little sharp. The two tunes sit together in the dark. The Clerk, who is tone-deaf and knows it, says only "the hour?" and Alder, glancing at the sky, calls "midnight," a full twenty minutes early. Nobody corrects him. Up on the hill, behind them, the parcel is still on the step, and the porch, which has had no lantern in living memory, is faintly gold on one side.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The charter says "the watch shall keep the wall," and Alder has read this as a limit as well as a duty. In forty years he has never set foot on the hill path, and he says "midnight" from the harbor side only. The customs house is the one place in Marrowby where the hour is never called. Whatever time it keeps up there, nobody has ever said it aloud.

**Consequence of yours:** The parcel is warm because something in it is warm on its own, and the tortoiseshell cat has noticed before anyone. When the men have gone, the cat stands, stretches, steps onto the brown paper and circles once. The knot, the one that holds, is under one paw. The cat lies down on the parcel and wraps itself around the small, shifting weight, with the folded ear against the paper, as if listening to something inside.

By sill custom, any creature may answer, and sleeping on a thing is a stronger touch than a paw. Against the grey flank of the stone the parcel's warmth is steady and quiet. The gold light of Alder's lantern slides along the harbor wall far below and, for a moment, reaches the porch step. The stone does not move, and the parcel does not stop being warm.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** Marrowby has a midwife, Ottoline Marsh, who has delivered most of the town's children and keeps no records except one habit: each baby's first sound is hummed to her by its mother, and Ottoline hums it back the next morning to the child, so that every Marrowby person has heard their own first note once and then forgotten it. She is nearly ninety, and has said she will teach the habit to nobody, because it only works if nobody is trying to keep it.

**Consequence of yours:** The cat sleeping on the parcel makes it the warmest thing on the hill. Near dawn, Ottoline, who has not slept past four in sixty years and takes her constitutional by the customs house, passes the porch and sees the tortoiseshell curled over a brown paper bundle with the stone beside it. She stops. She puts her head to one side, the way she does for a newborn, and listens.

What comes from the paper is not a sound exactly. It is the very smallest note, flat of the bell by a hair, and she knows it at once as a woman knows a hand she has held. She does not touch the parcel. She hums back, softly, the way she hums to infants, a single flat note, and the cat lifts its head to watch her do it. Then she walks home, entirely composed, and tells nobody, and puts the kettle on twice.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** Ottoline's own first note was never hummed back to her. Her mother died in the birth, and the midwife before her, an old woman named Dorrit Vane, was too grieved or too tired to carry the habit through. Ottoline has hummed ten thousand first notes to other people and has never heard her own. She has said, when pressed, only that it must have been a flat one, since she was born in Marrowby. It is the one entry in the town's strange accounting that she is missing, and she has never mentioned it to anyone.

**Consequence of yours:** Ottoline's habit has a cost she has hidden for ninety years, which is that every time she hums a baby's note back, she is also listening for a different one. The note from the parcel was a first note, she is sure of that, and she hummed it back out of long reflex. But she stands in her kitchen with two kettles going and cannot say whether it was a stranger's, or the child of a dead woman's, or hers. A first note can't be checked against anything. It exists only in the one person who made it and the one who hummed it back, and she is both a hummer and a person who was never hummed to.

She tries the note once, aloud, in the empty room, and the kettle's whistle answers a hair flat. She does not know whether she has found something or imitated it. She switches off the second kettle and sits down.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The midwife before Dorrit Vane was Hester's great-grandmother, and the Vane family's schoolloft above the baker's was originally a lying-in room, which is why the floor is warm and why the harmonium stands on the oldest board. The reed that was taken from the Vox Humana was not removed by a schoolmistress. It was removed by Dorrit, the night Ottoline was born, and nobody has ever asked her why. Dorrit died forty years ago, and Hester has never been told any of this.

**Consequence of yours:** Ottoline sits with the kettle gone quiet and a note in her mouth she can't place, and does the one thing she hasn't done in ninety years: she goes to ask someone. She walks to the schoolloft before the pupils come, climbs the stair, and finds Hester shoeless on the warm board with the half-drawn stop. Neither speaks first. The cat, who has followed Ottoline down the hill without being asked, steps onto the harmonium's lid.

Ottoline says only, "Pull it." Hester, who has wanted someone else to do it, does not say that. She looks at the old woman, then at the knob, and finds that being asked is different from wanting it done. She does not pull it, and does not refuse. The bellows leak their long sigh into the loft, and under the floor, through the flue, the baker stops kneading.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The baker's ovens were not built for bread. They were first lit to keep the lying-in room above them warm through winter births, and the bakery grew around the heat afterward, because a warm room is a useful thing to have underneath. The oldest oven has a plaque, worn blank, that was once a list of dates. The baker's family have always assumed the plaque was a recipe.

**Consequence of yours:** Ottoline, standing at the top of the loft stair with the cat at her heel, says nothing for a moment, and then she says it. "I was born on that board." She points, not at the harmonium but at the dark, slightly cupped plank beneath Hester's bare feet. "My mother died on it."

Hester, who has stood there every winter morning for years because it was warm, does not move. She looks down at the wood as if it had just said her name. The history she was told, that this was a loft above a bakery and nothing more, has been wrong for as long as she has taught here. She asks, carefully, whether Ottoline knows why the reed was taken. Ottoline says no, and neither of them touches the knob. Below the floor, through the flue grate, the baker has heard the word "born" and stopped. The ovens tick. The cat sits on the lid, a quarter-tone above the bell.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The baker's family keeps a book of its own, a baking log, in which each loaf's batch is recorded by date and weather. It has been kept for nine generations, and nobody outside the family has seen it. On certain dates, the oldest entries carry a small pencil mark beside the day, a short vertical stroke, which the baker has always taken for a flour-count tick. There are about three hundred strokes in nine generations, and one of them, from ninety years ago, is circled.

**Consequence of yours:** The baker, still at the grate, hears "I was born on that board" and wipes his hands on his apron without finishing the loaf. He does not go up. He goes to the shelf, takes down the baking log, and turns back through nine generations of weather and weight until he reaches the circled stroke, ninety years old, with a date beside it and nothing else.

He reads the date twice. He has no way of knowing whether it is Ottoline's birth, her mother's death, or only a batch that went wrong. A circle could mean any of them. He carries the book up the stair slowly, not as a man bringing proof, because a mark in a log cannot testify, but as a man bringing something that had been waiting in his house for ninety years to be asked about. In the doorway of the loft he stops, and the warm board, the old woman, the schoolmistress and the cat all look at the book in his hands.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The strokes in the baking log once meant something the family later forgot. On each marked day a small loaf was baked and left on the flue grate's ledge, unsold and unasked for, and by morning it was gone. The custom lapsed three generations back, when the ledge stopped being answered. The baker, who put a warm roll there on the morning of the vowel, did not know he was reviving it. He thought his hands had slipped.

**Consequence of yours:** The baker sets the book on the harmonium lid, open to the circled stroke, and nobody touches it. Ottoline reads the date over his arm, lips moving, and then says what she has always been told her birthday was. They are one day apart. The circle sits on the day after.

None of the four can say what it means. A midwife working through a death might have recorded it a day late. A baker might have left a loaf the morning after, as one did for a sorrow. Dorrit might have lied about the date, or the family had the date wrong ninety years ago and everyone since has repeated it. The cat steps onto the open page and sits squarely on the circle. Nobody moves him, and nobody reads the date aloud a second time.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** Marrowby has no gravestones. The dead are given to the estuary on the ebb in a plain flat boat, and the only marker is a knot tied in a length of string and looped over the harbor post for a day and a night. There are no records of whose knot is whose. Ottoline's mother was sent out this way, and the string would have been tied by Dorrit Vane. Nobody knows what the knot looked like.

**Consequence of yours:** The cat sits on the circle, the date is one day off, and Ottoline, who has never asked for anything, asks for one thing. "Does the post still have the loop?" she says. Hester doesn't know what she means. The baker does. The harbor post nearest the sparrows' stone still has a hollow worn in its side from ninety years of string, and one loop, very old, grey and brittle, that nobody has ever cut down.

They go down together, the four of them and the cat, in the thin light before the school fills. The loop is still there. The knot in it is a sixth kind, not hurried or patient or careful, and it has no third move that looks wrong. Tobias, coming up from the slip with a coil of rope, stops beside them. He looks at the knot for a long while. "That's not mine," he says, "and it's not the ferryman's." Ottoline touches it with one finger, and the tide, which has been out all morning, is exactly where it was.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The dead of Marrowby are sent out only on an ebb that follows a dry day. If a flood has come, the family waits, sometimes for several days, until the water has stood clean for a full tide. No one remembers who made the rule. It is understood that the estuary takes only what has not been lied about that day, which has caused real hardship in damp, talkative winters and has never once been challenged.

**Consequence of yours:** At the post, with the grey loop under her finger, Ottoline learns that Marrowby never records its dead, because the knot is the only record and nobody can say whose it is. Hester, who is good at dates, offers a thought: if Ottoline's mother died on the day of the birth, a flood might have delayed the sending, which would put the loop, and the baker's circle, a day later than the death. It sounds almost right. Ottoline shakes her head slowly. She was told she was born and her mother died on the same day, and a delay of one day would explain the circle but not the story she was given, so now there are two dates that cannot both be true and one old woman who has believed the wrong one, or the other, for ninety years.

She asks only that nobody cut the loop down. Tobias, without being asked, ties a new loop beside it in the one that holds, and leaves it empty. The tide comes in on schedule and washes neither.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** Tobias's new loop is not the first empty one. Beside the grey loop, on the far side of the post, are six others, each tied at a different time, in knots nobody has been able to read. They are neither old nor new, the string is plain and uncut, and each has been looped once and left. The town has always taken them for fishermen's tallies. Not one of the six has ever held a name.

**Consequence of yours:** Two dates that cannot both be true give Ottoline something she hasn't had in ninety years: a question that is hers. She does not ask Hester or the baker to resolve it. She goes home and does what the post taught her, and ties a knot of her own, not in string but in the corner of her apron, tight and plain, with no third move. She carries it for a day. It does not flood anything, because she says nothing, and she finds that the not-knowing sits more lightly when it has a shape.

At dusk she walks down again and looks at the seven empty loops, six old and one new, and ties her apron-knot's twin in a length of her own string, and loops it over the post beside them. It makes eight. It is, as far as she knows, the first knot in Marrowby tied by someone who is not mourning.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** Marrowby clears its harbor posts on the last day of winter. The custom is to cut every loop down and sweep the string into the ebb, "so the water can see." The grey loop has survived ninety years of clearings because, by an old habit, whoever holds the shears skips it without comment. Nobody knows who first started doing that, and the six unread loops have been skipped the same way. The shears are kept in the eel-sellers' cupboard and sharpened each autumn, and the last day of winter is nine days off.

**Consequence of yours:** Ottoline's loop is the eighth, and it has put the post's whole set of empty loops into the town's sight. Children, who know a sill when they see one, take it for a place to leave questions. By the weekend there are loops of every color of string. One for a lost cat, one for an unpaid debt, one for an argument between the eel-sellers about a stall boundary. Hester, passing, counts twenty-two and says nothing. She is not sure which of them are mourning.

The clearing is nine days off. Alder, doing his round on the harbor side of the wall, sees the gold of his lantern catch the loops in the dark and counts them without meaning to. He has a knot in his pocket that isn't his, and he stands at the post a little longer than the hour requires. The shears, in their cupboard, are very sharp. Whoever holds them this year will have to decide what to skip.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The shears have a keeper, chosen by lot on the last day of autumn: the eel-sellers draw a name from a bowl of tide-book scraps, and the person drawn holds the shears until the winter's end. This year's name was drawn two months ago and put away, and the eel-seller who drew it said only "free" when asked who it was. Nobody has pressed. The slip is folded in the cupboard under the shears' leather case, with the name unread.

**Consequence of yours:** Nine days is long enough for twenty-two loops to become sixty. People who never tied a knot in their lives tie one, and the post, which once held eight, bends under the weight of string. Hester's pupils start a game of reading them, and Perpetua, visiting on Thursday, is asked by several children what each one says and, for once, refuses. "That's not for reading," she says. "That's for leaving." She leaves her own, a plain overhand, tied without looking.

Wren, standing back, notices something none of the children have: the post has two sides. On the harbor side there are sixty loops. On the side facing the hill there are three, tied high, out of the reach of a child, and the string in them is the plain brown of the Hill's wrapper paper. Nobody has seen them added. By sill custom, anyone may answer. She does not go and look more closely, and she does not say anything.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The shears' leather case is older than the shears. The lining holds the pressed shape of a different tool, longer and thinner than any blade in town, with a small round hollow at one end. Nobody recognizes it. The eel-sellers oil the case each autumn and say it is "for the shears," and the shears fit it badly, rattling a little in the extra space.

**Consequence of yours:** With the keeper unread and the loops multiplying, the town starts guessing. The Clerk, who dislikes a blank space, writes "keeper, unread" in his margin and underlines it, which he rarely does. Corvin, passing the cupboard, offers in a thorough, reasonable voice to open the slip and read it aloud. The eel-seller, wiping a knife, says "tuppence," which is the price of a live rivalry. Corvin, who has counted the town's money for thirty years and never been told a price he couldn't pay, withdraws his offer and goes to sit on the wall with his thermos.

The guessing spreads. Some say the baker, some the sister, some Tobias, who would not hear his own name if it were shouted. Biscuit, the cat, is mentioned as a joke, and the eel-sellers laugh, in prices: "a penny." Nobody asks whether a cat can hold shears. The post leans a little further toward the sea, and the keeper, whoever it is, has seven days to decide what to skip.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The Hill-side loops have a pattern. There are three, and they are tied at the same height, a little above a tall man's reach, with the same plain brown paper cut into strips. The knot in each is the one that holds, tied correctly, third move and all. There is only one person in Marrowby who ties it that way unprompted, and he is deaf in one ear and has never been up to the post after dark.

**Consequence of yours:** The keeper's name stays folded, but the shears are taken out of the cupboard on the sixth day, and the eel-sellers do not say by whom. The sharpening stone, which lives beside them, is found damp. Somebody has been oiling the leather case too, as if preparing for a long use. The town, which watches for signs, reads the damp stone as an answer and cannot tell what it is.

Tobias, hearing about the three brown loops from a child, goes to the post at low tide with his good ear turned to the water. He looks at the knots for some time and says, quietly, that he did not tie them. The child asks who did. Tobias, who knows the knot has never been taught to anyone but a girl with the wrong hand and now half the wall, says, "Someone who was shown it right." Then he reaches up, as high as he can, and touches the nearest loop, and finds it is still warm.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The brown paper strips on the Hill-side loops have clean, straight edges, with no tearing and no fray. Each one has been cut, not ripped, with a stroke that did not hesitate. Paper cut that way leaves a faint dampness along the edge, as though the blade had been wet. Nobody in town has seen a blade like it, and the shears in the eel-sellers' cupboard, when they were taken out, were found to leave a ragged line.

**Consequence of yours:** Tobias is not the one who tied the knots, and he says so plainly, but his word cannot carry weight, because he is the only person in town who would, and a man who tells the truth about the one thing he'd be suspected of is still the suspect. The child who heard him murmurs that someone was shown it right. Wren, standing at the back of the small crowd with the four spans of cut string in her pocket, takes them out, because the clean wet end of it has been in her mind for weeks.

She holds it beside the nearest brown loop. The cuts match. The stroke is the same, the dampness the same, the edge as straight as if both had been taken in one pass. She cannot say what that means, only that the string that went out with the ice and the paper that came back on the hill came from the same blade. Tobias, watching her, says nothing. He has felt the loop's warmth, and she has felt the cut, and neither has found anything to put a name to.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The shape in the leather case's lining is a ferryman's blade, the kind used for cutting a boat free in an emergency. It is long and thin, with a round hollow in the handle for a thumb, and it was made to cut rope in one pull under tension. Tobias recognizes the outline the moment he sees it, because the ferryman before him wore one on a cord, and he was buried without it. Tobias has never owned one himself. Nobody had told him the knot and the blade came as a pair.

**Consequence of yours:** Wren's four spans and the three brown loops share a cut, and this is a fact nobody has a use for yet. She does not tell the town. She tells Tobias, because he is the only person who could do anything with it, and because he is already looking at the leather case where the eel-sellers have laid it on the harbor wall for the clearing.

He sets his thumb in the hollow of the lining. It fits. For sixty years he has used a knife that did the job and never wondered what the knot was a half of. Now he does, aloud, in front of a child, and the water stays flat. "If I'd had it," he says, "I'd have cut your string loose myself, that morning, before the ice took it." Wren, who has been wondering what cut it, does not answer. The tide, which has just turned, brings in nothing to the post, and the shears are still not accounted for.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** When the old ferryman was sent out on the ebb, the string looped on the post for him was not string. It was his own leather cord, the one he wore at his neck, tied off in the one that holds. It was the only marker anyone remembers that was not plain string, and nobody questioned it, because the dead are allowed their own things. The cord was found empty at the end of the day. The blade that should have hung from it had been taken off first, and nobody saw by whom.

**Consequence of yours:** The blade was buried, by the ferryman's own habit, with nothing: he was sent without it, and Tobias has always taken that as the old man's wish. But a man who wore a thing on a cord for sixty years does not slip it off on his last day for no reason, and Tobias, thumb still in the empty hollow of the lining, understands this at the same moment as the child beside him.

He goes to the post, to the six unread loops, and reaches past the plain string to the one that is not string. It is leather, dark and stiff, and the knot is his own, third move and all, tied by the one hand that ever tied it before him. At the lower end is a small, neat slit where a blade's ring once hung. It has been skipped at every clearing for forty years, by custom, by someone's mercy, and he is standing at it now, holding the cord up to the grey light, with the shears due in seven days and the blade nowhere in the harbor.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The Hill's three brown loops are not the only ones that have appeared without a tier. Every year on the last day of winter, after the clearing, one plain loop is found on the post by morning, tied in the one that holds, at a height only a tall person could reach. The town has always taken it for the keeper's own, left as a kind of receipt. The keeper, whoever is drawn, has always denied it, in the one way that never floods: by saying nothing.

**Consequence of yours:** Tobias holds the leather cord, with its slit and its empty ring, and says what he has never said at the post: "He took it off himself." The water does not rise. He means the ferryman, and means that the blade was not stolen, and that the old man knew, on his last morning, that someone would need it more than he did.

Wren asks who. Tobias says he doesn't know, but that it was never meant to wait forty years, and the blade has been used since. He looks at the straight, wet edge of the brown strips and says, "Not by me." Then he hangs the cord back on the post, exactly as it was, and ties nothing.

Across the harbor, the Inspector lands on the sparrows' stone, drinks from the seaward edge, and looks at the post. A dry morning is promised. The shears are in the cupboard, the slip is folded, and somewhere on the hill a cut is being made that nobody has asked for.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** Forty years ago, in a single dry week, Marrowby sent out two of its own: the old ferryman and Dorrit Vane, the midwife, one on the Monday ebb and one on the Thursday. The post held two loops that week, hers plain string and his leather cord. The town has always counted it as one hard winter and never as a coincidence. The first of the yearly receipt loops, by the best memory in town, appeared the following spring.

**Consequence of yours:** The yearly loop gets a different look once someone says its age aloud. Hester, working it out on her fingers outside the school, realizes that the keeper is drawn by lot every year and cannot be the same person twice, yet the knot is always tied identically, always high, always in the one that holds. A different keeper each year would not manage that. A different keeper each year would at least miss the third move once.

She says this to Wren, because Wren is nine and not yet afraid of it. Wren says that means the keeper isn't the one tying it, and that the shears and the loop are two different jobs. Hester agrees. Then she asks who is allowed to be on the hill side of the post at night, and Wren says the cats, and the watchman if he left the wall, and nobody else, because nobody has ever tried. The Inspector, drinking at the stone, takes off before they can decide whether to try.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The hill side of the post can only be reached at low tide, by a narrow shelf of rock that is wet and slick and barely a foot wide. Anyone walking it must face the post and sidestep. The shelf is undercut and sound, and since nobody has any reason to take it, it has acquired the status of a thing that exists only in principle. Children are told not to, and none have.

**Consequence of yours:** Wren decides to go, and tells Hester she will, because telling is a way of not being alone and a way of being stopped. Hester does not stop her. She says "low tide, and not alone," and Wren takes this as permission and also as a condition. At the next ebb they stand at the shelf's start, a girl and a schoolmistress with her shoes in her hand, looking at a foot of wet rock leading to a post with three brown loops on its far side.

They do not cross. They watch the water slide out, and about a body-length along the shelf, at the height of a hand, they see a small pale mark scratched into the stone. It is a short vertical stroke, like the baker's pencil ticks, and under it there is a second, and a third. Dozens. A tally of something, going back and back, until the lowest strokes are weathered smooth. Neither of them says "that's the baking log." Neither of them says anything. The tide comes back in on schedule, and the shelf goes under, and the strokes with it.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** In winter, Marrowby's lowest ebbs fall after dark, and the shelf behind the post is bare for no more than ten minutes at a stretch. In summer the same tide comes at midday and gives half an hour. The town has always called the winter tide "the short one" and never worked out that it hides the hill side of the post from everyone who isn't looking for it.

**Consequence of yours:** Hester and Wren agree, on the walk back, to count the strokes. They cannot do it by daylight, so they will have to do it by lamp in the ten minutes the winter tide allows, with a slick foot of rock under them and the sea waiting at both ends. Hester does not like it. She says so, and goes on planning anyway, with the particular calm of someone who has decided and is waiting to be argued out of it.

She needs oil, and the only oil that will make a lamp useful for reading marks on wet stone is the guild's. She goes, awkwardly, to the lamplighters' porch, where the apprentice who has been writing "two climbers, one dry" in the porch ledger is sweeping. The girl asks nothing. She fills a small flask and hands it over, and Hester offers payment, and the apprentice says, "I'll put it down as weather." Hester does not know what that means. She carries the flask home warm in her pocket, and the apprentice goes back to sweeping, a little lighter than before.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**New fact:** The guild's oil, burned on wet stone, shows green where the stone has ever been touched by floodwater and nothing where it hasn't. This is an old guild secret that Odessa's predecessors never sold, since a monopoly on oil that shows nothing is worth more than one that shows too much. It means the shelf, which every flood crosses, should glow all along its length, and the strokes should glow brightest where the water has carried something over them longest.

**Consequence of yours:** On the first winter ebb, Hester and Wren go out with the flask, a shielded lamp, and a plan to count to ten minutes by Wren's breathing. The rock is as slick as promised. They sidestep, and the lamp, set low, makes the shelf glow a faint dull green, solid as a road. Under it the strokes stand out, pale on green, dozens of them, in groups of five with a diagonal through each.

They count forty-one groups before the water begins to lap at the shelf's far end. Wren counts the last row twice and is sure of it. Hester does not say the number aloud, because it matches no date she knows: the baking log's strokes number about three hundred, and these number more than two hundred. The tide comes in. They walk back along a road that is already going under, lamp low, and the green fades behind them, leaving the stone dark and the post upright, and the three brown loops swinging on the far side.

Your turn: add a fact and a consequence of mine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**New fact:** The flat boat used for sendings is kept under the ferry shed, and it is launched from the slip, never the shelf. Tobias has handled it at every sending for sixty years, and the shelf behind the post has never been part of the rite. Nobody has ever needed it. Children are warned off the rock because it is slick, and the warning has done so well that grown people have also forgotten it exists.

**Consequence of yours:** The oil shows the strokes plainly, and also shows what they are not. Hester, thinking it over, takes the count to Ottoline, who has stood at more sendings than anyone alive, and asks whether two hundred and five could be the dead. Ottoline thinks a long time and says that in ninety years she has seen perhaps a hundred and fifty, that the nine generations before would add more, and that the number could fit, but that every one of them left from the slip and no one ever stood on the shelf.

"Then someone counted them from behind," says Hester, and Ottoline says nothing. It is not a reproach. Neither of them says what it would mean to tally the dead from the hill side of the post, at ten minutes of low tide, in the dark, with a blade that cuts clean. The strokes that Wren counted twice were not all the same age. The last three, at the high end of the row, were not weathered at all.
